# iTerm Organizer

Portfolio copy for kodefoundry. Three lengths, pick what fits the layout.

**Name:** iTerm Organizer
**Tagline:** Session recovery for iTerm2
**Icon:** `docs/assets/icon-1024.png` (also 512 and 256; generated by `packaging/make_icon.py`)
**Screenshots:** `docs/assets/screenshot-hero.png` (icon and restore prompt on a dark card),
`docs/assets/screenshot-restore-prompt.png` (the dialog alone, transparent corners)
**Stack:** Python 3.11, iTerm2 Python API, launchd, pytest, macOS app bundle with ad-hoc code signing

## One line

A macOS background agent that snapshots your iTerm2 windows, tabs and split
panes every minute, then offers to rebuild them after a crash or a restart.

## Card blurb

iTerm Organizer saves the shape of your terminal every 60 seconds: window
geometry, the split tree, each pane's folder, profile, git branch and running
command. When iTerm2 comes back from a reboot or a crash, it offers to put all
of it back.

## Long description

Lose power mid-afternoon and iTerm2 reopens empty. Six windows, a dozen panes,
four repos on four branches, and no record of what any of them was doing. I
built iTerm Organizer so that stops being a problem.

It runs as a launchd agent wired to iTerm2's Python API. Every 60 seconds it
walks the window and pane tree and writes a snapshot: window position and size,
the nested split layout, and per pane the working directory, profile, title,
git branch and the command actually running there. On the next fresh iTerm2
instance it asks once whether to rebuild. Every restored pane opens with a
one-line banner reminding you where you were, and the last 20 distinct
snapshots are archived, so you can go back to an hour ago rather than just to
the last save.

Replaying a command read out of the process table is code execution at login,
so it's gated. Only exact allowlist matches run by themselves, things like
`npm run dev` or `claude --continue`. A deny list covering `ssh`, `sudo` and
`git rebase` is checked first and never runs. Everything else gets typed into
the pane and waits for you to press Enter.

### The parts that were actually hard

Finding the real command in a pane. iTerm2 reports a job pid, but it points at
the deepest foreground process, so a pane running Claude Code reports one of
the MCP helpers Claude spawned. The daemon instead walks down the process tree
from the session's own shell and takes the shallowest descendant that isn't a
shell, covering every pane in one `ps` call.

Getting a background job talking to iTerm2 at all. Connecting needs an auth
cookie the iterm2 library requests over AppleScript, and for a launchd job with
no bundle identity macOS blocks that behind a permission prompt that never
appears. The agent hangs forever with no error. Declaring
`AssociatedBundleIdentifiers = com.googlecode.iterm2` in the job definition is
what lets it through.

Deciding when to ask. At login launchd starts the agent before iTerm2 exists,
so anything measured up front is meaningless, and window counts are useless
because iTerm2 reopens its own windows after a reboot. Restore is keyed on
iTerm2's process id instead, decided after connecting, offered once per
instance.

### Engineering notes

Every iTerm2 API call lives in one module and the rest is pure and testable
without iTerm2 running, which is how 184 tests cover snapshot capture, tier
classification and restore planning offline. Snapshots are written to a temp
file and moved into place with `os.replace`, with the previous copy kept
alongside, and an empty snapshot never overwrites a good one. A `flock`
guarantees a single daemon, and the kernel drops it on crash, which matters
since crashing is the case the tool exists for.

Ships as a 4 MB signed app bundle with a generated icon, carrying its own
dependencies and running on any Python 3.11 or newer already on the machine.
Double-click to install.
